question: A self-employed client could cover living expenses for 90 days if unable to work. When selecting disability insurance, which elimination period most closely matches that reserve?
options: 0 days
30 days
90 days
2 years
explanation: The elimination period is the waiting period after disability begins before benefits become payable. A 90-day emergency reserve can support a 90-day waiting period, subject to the client's risk tolerance.

question: What does the benefit period in a disability income policy describe?
options: How long the insured must wait before applying
The maximum period benefits can be payable for a qualifying disability
How long underwriting remains valid
The period during which premiums are refunded
explanation: The benefit period is the maximum duration for which disability benefits may be paid for a covered disability, subject to the contract.

question: A surgeon can no longer perform surgery because of a hand injury but can teach medicine. Which disability definition generally provides the strongest protection for the surgeon's specialized occupation?
options: Any occupation
Own occupation
Presumptive disability only
Loss-of-income exclusion
explanation: An own-occupation definition focuses on the insured's ability to perform the important duties of the occupation held when disability began. Exact wording varies by contract.

question: Why is an 'any occupation' disability definition generally harder to satisfy than an own-occupation definition?
options: It requires hospitalization
It considers the ability to work in another occupation for which the insured is reasonably suited under the contract
It applies only to accidents
It requires permanent paralysis
explanation: Any-occupation wording broadens the work the insured may be expected to perform. Policies differ in how education, training, experience and earnings are considered.

question: A disabled consultant returns to work part-time and earns 50% of pre-disability income. Which policy feature is designed to provide a proportionate benefit for continuing income loss?
options: Residual disability benefit
Accidental death benefit
Future purchase option
Hospital indemnity benefit
explanation: Residual or partial disability provisions can pay a reduced benefit when the insured works but continues to experience a qualifying loss of income.

question: What is the purpose of a cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) rider on disability insurance?
options: Increase benefits during a long claim to help offset inflation
Shorten the elimination period automatically
Refund premiums every year
Increase benefits whenever salary rises before disability
explanation: A COLA rider generally adjusts benefits after disability has begun according to the rider's formula or inflation measure, helping preserve purchasing power during a long claim.

question: A young professional expects income to rise substantially and wants the right to buy more disability coverage later without new medical evidence. Which feature is most relevant?
options: Future increase option
Return-of-premium provision
Coordination-of-benefits clause
Recurrent disability provision
explanation: A future increase or future purchase option protects medical insurability by allowing additional coverage at specified times, usually subject to financial underwriting and contractual limits.

question: Which statement best distinguishes guaranteed renewable disability insurance from non-cancellable coverage?
options: Guaranteed renewable coverage may permit class-wide premium changes; non-cancellable coverage generally locks contractual premiums and benefits while required premiums are paid
Guaranteed renewable policies may be cancelled whenever the insured becomes ill
Non-cancellable policies never have exclusions
There is no practical difference
explanation: Guaranteed renewable contracts generally restrict individual cancellation but may allow premium changes for an entire class. Non-cancellable wording usually adds stronger premium and benefit guarantees, subject to the contract.

question: A client pays 100% of the premiums for an individual disability income policy personally. What is the usual Canadian tax treatment of benefits?
options: Benefits are generally received tax-free
Benefits are always employment income
Only the first year is tax-free
Benefits are capital gains
explanation: When an individual personally pays the full disability premium with after-tax dollars, benefits are generally received tax-free. Tax treatment can differ for employer-sponsored arrangements.

question: An employer pays the premiums for an employee wage-loss replacement disability plan. What is the general tax consequence when periodic disability benefits are paid?
options: Benefits are generally taxable to the employee, subject to the applicable tax rules
Benefits are always tax-free
Premiums become a capital loss
Benefits are treated as dividends
explanation: Where an employer contributes to a wage-loss replacement plan, periodic benefits are generally taxable, with employee contributions potentially relevant to the calculation under the tax rules.

question: Why do disability insurers limit the amount of income replacement available?
options: To reduce overinsurance and preserve an incentive to return to work
Because benefits may never exceed 25% of income
Because only mortgage payments may be insured
Because all disability benefits are taxable
explanation: Disability coverage normally replaces only part of earned income. Insurers consider existing coverage and other benefits to reduce overinsurance and moral hazard.

question: A client already has employer long-term disability coverage. Before recommending an individual policy, what should the advisor determine first?
options: The amount, definition of disability, waiting period, benefit period, offsets and portability of the existing plan
Only the employer's name
Only whether the client has life insurance
The client's preferred investment fund
explanation: Existing group coverage must be understood before identifying a disability-income gap. Group benefits may have different definitions, limits, offsets and termination rules.

question: Which client generally has the greatest need for individually owned disability income insurance?
options: A self-employed professional whose lifestyle depends on earned income and who has limited employer benefits
A retired person with no employment income and a fully funded pension
A child with no earned income
A corporation seeking property insurance
explanation: Disability income insurance protects earning capacity. A self-employed person with substantial earned-income dependence and little group protection has a significant exposure.

question: A business owner wants insurance to reimburse fixed business expenses such as rent and certain employee salaries if the owner becomes disabled. Which product is designed for this need?
options: Business overhead expense disability insurance
Personal health spending account
Accidental death insurance
Travel medical insurance
explanation: Business overhead expense coverage is intended to reimburse eligible ongoing business expenses during a qualifying disability; it is not primarily personal income replacement.

question: Two partners have an agreement requiring one partner's interest to be purchased if that partner becomes permanently disabled. Which insurance need does this create?
options: Disability buy-sell funding
Hospital indemnity coverage
Travel cancellation coverage
Dental reimbursement
explanation: Disability buy-sell insurance can provide funding for a purchase obligation triggered by a qualifying disability under a properly coordinated agreement.

question: What is the main purpose of key-person disability insurance?
options: Help a business absorb financial loss when an important employee or owner is disabled
Replace every employee's provincial health plan
Pay the disabled person's personal mortgage directly
Fund retirement benefits at age 65
explanation: Key-person disability coverage is a business-protection tool intended to compensate the business for losses associated with a key person's disability.

question: An applicant works at heights and participates in high-risk recreational aviation. Why are these facts relevant to disability underwriting?
options: Occupation and avocations can materially affect the probability and severity of a disability claim
They determine the beneficiary designation
They automatically make benefits tax-free
They affect only life insurance, not disability insurance
explanation: Disability underwriting considers occupation, duties and hazardous activities because these can affect claim risk. The insurer may adjust premiums, benefits or exclusions accordingly.

question: An insurer excludes claims arising from a client's pre-existing knee condition but covers otherwise eligible disabilities. What underwriting action has occurred?
options: A specific impairment exclusion
A beneficiary change
A policy loan
A coordination-of-benefits payment
explanation: A specific exclusion removes or limits coverage for a defined condition while leaving other covered causes of disability insured.

question: What is the main purpose of a waiver-of-premium provision in disability insurance?
options: Waive required premiums during a qualifying disability after the contractual waiting period
Increase the insured's salary
Eliminate all policy exclusions
Pay medical bills directly
explanation: Waiver of premium helps keep coverage in force without ongoing premium payments while the insured satisfies the policy's disability requirements.

question: A disability recurs shortly after the insured returns to work. Why is a recurrent-disability provision important?
options: It may treat the recurrence as part of the prior claim so a new elimination period is not required, subject to the contract
It guarantees a larger benefit
It converts disability insurance to critical illness insurance
It eliminates medical evidence from every future claim
explanation: Recurrent-disability clauses define when a returning disability is treated as a continuation of an earlier claim rather than a new disability.

question: A policy provides a presumptive disability benefit for specified catastrophic losses. What is the usual purpose of this provision?
options: Treat specified severe losses as total disability without requiring the ordinary occupational test to be met
Pay only if the insured returns to work
Replace provincial health coverage
Shorten every policy's elimination period to zero
explanation: Presumptive disability provisions commonly identify severe losses, such as certain losses of sight, hearing, speech or limbs, that qualify under special contractual rules.

question: A client receives disability income from more than one source. What is the purpose of an offset or coordination provision?
options: Prevent combined benefits from exceeding the level permitted by the contract
Make all benefits tax-free
Extend the benefit period automatically
Remove the definition of disability
explanation: Many disability plans coordinate with other disability income sources. The policy specifies which amounts reduce the insurer's benefit and how the calculation works.

question: Which public program may provide long-term disability income to a contributor who meets a severe and prolonged disability test under federal rules?
options: CPP disability benefit, or QPP disability under Quebec's system
Old Age Security only
GST/HST credit
Canada Education Savings Grant
explanation: CPP and QPP provide disability benefits to qualifying contributors under their respective statutory tests. Private insurance should be assessed alongside available public benefits.

question: Why should an advisor not assume CPP/QPP disability benefits will fully replace a client's private disability-insurance need?
options: Eligibility tests and benefit amounts differ from private contracts and may leave a substantial income gap
CPP/QPP covers only accidental disability
CPP/QPP benefits are available to everyone regardless of contributions
Private disability benefits are prohibited when CPP/QPP exists
explanation: Government disability programs have statutory eligibility and benefit formulas. They should be considered in the needs analysis, not assumed to provide complete income replacement.

question: A worker is injured in the course of employment and receives workers' compensation benefits. How are these benefits generally treated for federal income-tax purposes?
options: They are generally not taxable, although they are reported and can affect certain calculations
They are always taxed as employment income
They are capital gains
They are deductible premiums
explanation: Workers' compensation benefits are generally not taxable, but recipients report them on the tax return because they can affect certain credits and benefit calculations.

question: What is the principal role of provincial or territorial health insurance when evaluating a client's accident and sickness needs?
options: It establishes the base public medical coverage, while private insurance may address eligible expenses and risks not fully covered
It replaces all disability income
It guarantees out-of-country medical coverage without limits
It pays a lump sum for every critical illness
explanation: Public health plans cover many medically necessary services, but private accident and sickness products can address gaps such as drugs, dental, travel emergencies or income loss, depending on the plan.

question: A client has no employer health benefits and regularly pays for prescription drugs, dental care and paramedical services. Which product is most directly designed to help with these costs?
options: Supplementary health and dental insurance
Disability buy-sell insurance
Key-person life insurance
An immediate annuity
explanation: Supplementary health and dental plans reimburse eligible medical and dental expenses according to their deductibles, coinsurance, maximums and exclusions.

question: A health plan has an annual $100 deductible. What does this generally mean?
options: The insured pays the first $100 of eligible expenses before the plan begins reimbursing according to its terms
The insurer pays the first $100 only
Every claim is reduced by exactly $100 forever
The annual premium is $100
explanation: A deductible is the amount the insured must absorb before eligible reimbursement begins. The exact application may be individual, family, annual or per claim depending on the contract.

question: A plan reimburses 80% of eligible drug expenses after the deductible. What does the remaining 20% represent?
options: The insured's coinsurance share
A policy dividend
A disability elimination period
A premium refund
explanation: Coinsurance splits eligible expenses between insurer and insured. With 80% reimbursement, the insured normally bears 20%, subject to plan limits.

question: Two spouses each have employer health plans covering the family. Why is coordination of benefits used?
options: To determine the order of payment and prevent reimbursement above the eligible expense while allowing coverage from both plans
To cancel one spouse's plan automatically
To make every expense fully reimbursable regardless of plan limits
To determine disability occupation class
explanation: Coordination-of-benefits rules establish which plan pays first and how the second plan considers the remaining eligible amount, without allowing total reimbursement above the expense.

question: An employer pays premiums for qualifying private health services plan coverage for an employee. How are eligible medical benefits paid under that plan generally treated for the employee?
options: They are generally non-taxable
They are always taxable salary
They are capital dividends
They are taxable only if a deductible applies
explanation: CRA generally treats eligible medical benefits paid under a qualifying private health services plan as non-taxable to the employee, subject to the applicable rules.

question: Why is travel medical insurance particularly important for a Canadian travelling outside the country?
options: Provincial or territorial coverage may reimburse only a limited amount of out-of-country medical costs, leaving potentially large expenses
Provincial coverage automatically pays every foreign hospital bill in full
Travel insurance guarantees entry into every country
Travel insurance replaces the traveller's passport
explanation: Emergency medical care abroad can be very expensive and public-plan reimbursement may be limited. Travel medical insurance can cover eligible emergency expenses subject to exclusions and limits.

question: A traveller had recent treatment for a heart condition before departure. What policy provision should be reviewed especially carefully before relying on travel medical coverage?
options: The pre-existing-condition stability requirement
The disability benefit period
The life-insurance suicide clause
The annuity guarantee period
explanation: Travel policies commonly contain stability periods or exclusions for pre-existing medical conditions. The exact definition and required stable period must be checked before travel.

question: A traveller becomes seriously ill overseas. Why should the traveller contact the travel insurer's assistance centre as soon as reasonably possible?
options: The insurer may coordinate care, confirm eligible facilities and apply notification or pre-authorization requirements
Calling guarantees every expense will be paid
The assistance centre replaces all physicians
The call converts the policy into disability insurance
explanation: Emergency-assistance services can coordinate treatment and payment. Policies may also require prompt notification or authorization for certain services, so clients should know the procedure before travelling.

question: What is the fundamental difference between critical illness insurance and disability income insurance?
options: Critical illness generally pays a lump sum when a covered condition and contract requirements are met; disability insurance replaces part of income during a qualifying disability
Both pay only medical receipts
Critical illness pays only if the insured cannot work
Disability insurance pays only after death
explanation: Critical illness is diagnosis/condition based and typically pays a lump sum, while disability income coverage focuses on the insured's inability to work or loss of income under the contract.

question: A client asks whether every critical illness policy uses the same 30-day survival period for every covered condition. What is the best response?
options: No. Survival periods and other requirements are contract- and condition-specific and must be verified in the policy
Yes, 30 days is mandatory for every condition in Canada
No critical illness policy has a survival period
Survival periods apply only to disability insurance
explanation: Critical illness contracts differ. Some covered conditions may have survival periods, waiting periods or other definitions that vary by insurer and condition.

question: A client survives a covered critical illness and receives a lump-sum benefit. What restriction is usually placed on how the client spends the benefit?
options: Generally none; once payable, the lump sum can usually be used for any purpose
It must be paid only to a hospital
It must be used to replace salary dollar-for-dollar
It must be invested in an RRSP
explanation: Critical illness benefits are generally lump-sum payments that are not tied to specific medical receipts, giving the insured flexibility to address treatment, recovery, debt or other needs.

question: Why is it misleading to advertise a generic critical illness policy as covering '25+ conditions' without qualification?
options: The number and definitions of covered conditions vary by product, and coverage depends on satisfying the specific contract definition
Canadian law limits every policy to three conditions
All policies cover exactly the same illnesses
Condition counts determine disability tax treatment
explanation: Critical illness products vary widely. Exam preparation should focus on contract definitions, exclusions and suitability rather than presenting one condition count as universal.

question: What does accidental death and dismemberment (AD&D) insurance generally cover?
options: Specified losses resulting from a covered accident, according to a schedule and policy terms
All deaths from illness
Routine dental expenses
Loss of employment for any reason
explanation: AD&D coverage pays for covered accidental death or specified accidental losses such as certain losses of limbs or senses, subject to definitions and exclusions.

question: Why should AD&D coverage not be treated as a substitute for comprehensive life or disability insurance?
options: It responds only to covered accidental events and therefore leaves illness and many other causes uninsured
It always costs more than comprehensive insurance
It cannot name a beneficiary
It is available only to corporations
explanation: Accidents are only one source of death or disability. Broader life and disability coverage addresses risks that AD&D alone does not cover.

question: A hospital indemnity policy pays $200 per day of covered hospitalization regardless of the hospital's actual bill. What type of benefit is this?
options: A stated or indemnity-style cash benefit based on the contract, not reimbursement of actual expenses
Coinsurance reimbursement
A disability buyout
A policy loan
explanation: Hospital cash plans can pay a fixed amount for qualifying hospitalization rather than reimbursing the exact medical expense incurred.

question: What is the purpose of a maximum benefit provision in supplementary health insurance?
options: Limit the insurer's payment for a specified service, period or lifetime according to the contract
Guarantee unlimited reimbursement
Set the client's employment income
Determine the disability elimination period
explanation: Health plans often impose annual, per-service or lifetime maximums. These limits are important when evaluating whether existing coverage meets the client's needs.

question: A client is comparing two disability policies. Policy A has a 30-day elimination period and Policy B has a 120-day period, with all else similar. Which policy would normally cost more?
options: Policy A, because benefits can begin sooner
Policy B, because the insured waits longer
They must cost exactly the same
Neither policy charges premiums
explanation: A shorter elimination period exposes the insurer to earlier and potentially more claims, so it generally increases premium relative to a longer waiting period.

question: Two otherwise similar disability policies provide benefits for 2 years and to age 65 respectively. Which generally has the higher premium?
options: The policy with benefits potentially payable to age 65
The 2-year policy
They must have identical premiums
The shorter policy because it pays fewer claims
explanation: A longer potential benefit period creates greater insurer exposure and generally costs more, all other underwriting and contract features being equal.

question: A client earns $8,000 per month and has employer disability coverage of $4,000 per month. Why might an insurer refuse to issue another $8,000 monthly individual benefit?
options: Total coverage could exceed reasonable income-replacement limits and create overinsurance
Individual policies may never supplement group insurance
Monthly benefits must equal mortgage payments
The client already has health insurance
explanation: Insurers financially underwrite disability benefits against earned income and existing coverage. The goal is meaningful replacement without creating an incentive to remain disabled.

question: Which source of income is most relevant when financially underwriting an individual disability income policy for a self-employed person?
options: Documented earned income attributable to the client's work, assessed under the insurer's rules
The market value of the client's home only
Expected inheritance
Credit-card limit
explanation: Disability income insurance protects earned income. Self-employed applicants often need financial documentation because gross business revenue is not the same as personal insurable earnings.

question: An insured intentionally fails to disclose a material medical condition on an accident and sickness application. What is the primary concern?
options: Material misrepresentation can affect coverage and may lead to denial or rescission according to the contract and applicable law
The insurer must ignore the omission
The policy automatically becomes non-cancellable
Only the premium payment date matters
explanation: Accurate disclosure is fundamental to underwriting. Material misrepresentation or non-disclosure can jeopardize the contract or a claim, subject to applicable law.

question: A disability claimant has met the elimination period. What should determine whether benefits are payable next?
options: Whether the claimant satisfies the policy's definition of disability and other claim requirements
Whether the claimant owns life insurance
Whether interest rates increased
Whether the beneficiary is revocable
explanation: Completing the waiting period alone does not establish entitlement. The claimant must satisfy the contractual disability definition and ongoing proof requirements.

question: Why can a rehabilitation benefit be valuable in a disability policy?
options: It can support an appropriate return-to-work or retraining plan under the policy, potentially improving recovery and earning capacity
It guarantees lifetime benefits
It removes every exclusion
It pays a death benefit
explanation: Some disability contracts support rehabilitation or retraining when appropriate. The objective is to help the insured regain functional or vocational capacity.

question: A disability policy changes from an own-occupation definition for the first 24 months to an any-occupation definition afterward. What should the client understand?
options: Continuing eligibility may become harder after 24 months because a broader range of suitable work can be considered
Benefits automatically double after 24 months
The policy terminates after 24 months
The elimination period starts again every month
explanation: Many group and some individual contracts change definitions after a stated period. A claimant who qualifies initially may not satisfy the later, stricter definition.

question: A client is offered a disability policy with a return-of-premium feature at a materially higher cost. What should the advisor emphasize?
options: Evaluate the added cost, conditions for receiving the refund and whether core disability protection is adequately funded first
The refund is guaranteed regardless of claims or policy conditions
Return of premium always improves the disability definition
The feature makes benefits tax-deductible
explanation: Optional refund features can be attractive but should not displace adequate core coverage. Their conditions, opportunity cost and effect on affordability should be evaluated.

question: A client with six months of emergency savings is choosing between a richer monthly disability benefit and a shorter elimination period. Which planning principle is most appropriate?
options: Use available savings to assess how much waiting-period risk the client can retain, then prioritize adequate long-term income replacement
Always choose the shortest waiting period regardless of cost
Always choose the longest waiting period
Ignore emergency savings
explanation: An emergency fund can cover part of a disability waiting period. Matching retained risk to available liquidity can make premiums more efficient while preserving long-term protection.

question: A client is retiring next month and will no longer rely on employment earnings. What should an advisor consider when reviewing an individual disability income policy?
options: The original income-replacement need may be ending, so continuation or termination should be reviewed against contract terms and remaining needs
Disability coverage must always be increased at retirement
The policy automatically becomes critical illness insurance
Retirement has no relevance to disability-income needs
explanation: Disability income insurance primarily protects earned income. Retirement can materially change the exposure, although termination decisions should consider contract rights and the client's full circumstances.

question: A client leaves an employer and loses group health and disability coverage. What is the advisor's best immediate action?
options: Identify termination dates, any conversion or continuation rights, and the new gaps before recommending replacement coverage
Assume all group benefits continue for life
Cancel all existing individual coverage
Wait until the client has a claim
explanation: Loss of employment can create immediate insurance gaps. Deadlines for conversion or continuation may be short, so existing rights and new needs should be reviewed promptly.

question: A client wants critical illness insurance mainly because a serious diagnosis could require a spouse to take unpaid leave and create travel or home-care costs. Why can CI insurance fit this need?
options: A qualifying lump-sum benefit can provide flexible liquidity for indirect costs that ordinary health insurance may not reimburse
CI insurance reimburses only prescription receipts
CI insurance replaces provincial health coverage
CI insurance guarantees recovery
explanation: The flexibility of a lump-sum critical illness benefit can help fund non-medical and indirect costs arising from a covered diagnosis, provided the contract's definition is satisfied.

question: A client asks whether a diagnosis described colloquially as 'cancer' guarantees a critical illness claim. What should the advisor explain?
options: No. The diagnosis must meet the policy's precise covered-condition definition and any waiting, survival or exclusion requirements
Yes. Any use of the word cancer guarantees payment
Only the client's physician decides whether the insurer must pay
Critical illness policies never define cancer
explanation: Critical illness claims depend on contractual definitions. Some forms or stages of disease may be excluded or treated differently, so the actual wording controls.

question: An employer pays the premium for an employee's group critical illness insurance. Which tax issue should be checked rather than assuming the arrangement is tax-free?
options: Employer-paid premiums for group sickness or accident coverage that provides lump-sum benefits can be a taxable employee benefit under CRA rules
Critical illness premiums can never create a taxable benefit
Only disability waiting periods affect taxation
The employee must report the death benefit as salary
explanation: CRA distinguishes group sickness or accident plans and wage-loss replacement plans. Employer contributions for lump-sum coverage such as critical illness may create a taxable benefit to the employee.

question: Which recommendation best follows the LLQP approach when a client has several accident and sickness risks?
options: Assess the client's situation and existing public, group and individual coverage, identify gaps, then recommend products matched to those gaps
Recommend the product with the highest commission
Use the same disability amount for every client
Ignore existing employer benefits
explanation: Suitability begins with the client's needs and existing resources. Product selection follows the gap analysis rather than preceding it.

question: A client wants to cancel an old individual disability policy immediately after applying for a new one. What is the safest advice?
options: Keep existing coverage until the new policy is issued, delivered and accepted as appropriate, and review any replacement consequences before cancelling
Cancel immediately to avoid duplicate coverage
Assume the new application guarantees approval
Stop paying premiums before underwriting is complete
explanation: New coverage is not guaranteed merely because an application was submitted. Replacement should be handled carefully so the client does not unintentionally lose valuable protection.

question: A 42-year-old self-employed consultant earns $120,000, has three months of savings, no group benefits, two children and a mortgage. Which is the best first step in designing accident and sickness coverage?
options: Quantify the income and medical-expense risks, review public coverage and savings, then select disability, health and other products according to the identified gaps
Buy the maximum critical illness policy first without analysis
Use only the mortgage balance to set every benefit
Choose the disability policy with the shortest elimination period regardless of budget
explanation: A comprehensive needs analysis considers income replacement, emergency reserves, public benefits, health-expense exposure, family obligations and affordability before products and riders are selected.
